title: Heuristic Play
strapline: Tins, tubes, chains and corks — an hour of serious research for toddlers who need to find out what things do.
intent: Give mobile babies and toddlers open-ended materials with no right answer — everything is for finding out.
Feed the big fascinations of this age: filling and emptying, posting, stacking, hiding and finding.
Develop hand skills and whole-body effort — lifting heavy tins, threading chains, prising off lids.
Protect long, uninterrupted concentration in a calm room where the adult is quiet and the materials do the talking.
Grow independence and determination: the child sets the problem, works at it, and solves it themselves.
Build the earliest logic — which things fit, which things roll, which things are the same.
implementation: Set up before the children arrive: clusters of one material each — tins, cardboard tubes, chains, corks, curtain rings, large pegs, fabric bags — spread across a clear floor.
Sit low, stay quiet and stay put — in heuristic play the adult is a calm anchor, not a commentator; save the rich talk for afterwards.
Resist rescuing: when the lid won't come off or the chain misses the tin, wait — the working-out is the whole point.
Watch each child's schema and quietly plan for it — more tubes for the poster, more bags for the transporter, more lids for the twister.
Keep the session unhurried (30–60 minutes) and end with tidying as part of the play — sorting everything back into its own bag.
Refresh and check materials weekly: rusty tins out, sharp edges out, anything mouthable kept generously sized.
Afterwards, tell the story back to the child and their family: 'You filled the tin with corks and tipped it out eleven times.'
key_questions: Will the chain fit through the tube — where did it go?
Which tin does the big lid belong to?
How many corks can the little bag hold before they spill?
Where could the pom-pom be hiding?
That tin sounds different with the chain inside — can you hear it?
The tower fell down — what will you do now?

impact.text: Toddlers fill tins with corks and tip them out, post chains through tubes, stack and nest and hide and find — the same experiment run again and again on purpose.
Children work out how things work by trying: twisting lids off tins, pushing rings onto the mug tree, testing which objects fit through which tube.
A toddler drops a chain into a tin, listens, tips it out and does it again — making sounds on purpose and clearly relishing the effect.
Children haul, carry and push the heavy things deliberately — a bag of chains lugged across the room, the big tin pushed to a new workspace.
Children group the materials by their own logic — all the corks in one tin, every chain gathered into one lap.
A child bats away help with the stuck lid — 'me do it!' — works on, and glows with pride when it finally gives.
Early quantity and size words surface at the tins: 'more', 'all gone', 'big one' — and at tidy-up, children name what they're bagging.
Because their key person stays calm and close, even the youngest explorers range out across the materials and check back with a look, not a cry.

enhancements: A mug tree with curtain rings and hair scrunchies — on, off, on again.
Tins in graduated sizes so nesting and lid-matching become the puzzle.
Lengths of chain in different weights — fine and delicate, heavy and clanking.
Cardboard tubes taped to the wall at toddler height with a basket of pom-poms and corks below — post at the top, catch at the bottom.
Fabric bags with drawstrings — filling, dragging, and the fine-motor puzzle of the string itself.
Large wooden dolly pegs to clip around a tin rim or drop through a tube.
A session with everything cylindrical — tubes, tins, corks, rolling pins — and watch the rolling research begin.

playing_exploring: Children roam the materials freely, combining tins with chains with tubes in ways no adult planned.
Objects are tested with hands, mouths, ears and full body weight — real research with real stuff.
active_learning: Toddlers repeat an action dozens of times, refining it — the chain misses the tube, misses, then goes in clean.
Stuck lids and toppled towers are met with another go, not a request for rescue.
creating_thinking: Children invent their own problems to solve: can the big tin wear the little tin as a hat, will every cork fit in the bag?
They notice what their experiments teach them and change approach — turning the tube, choosing the bigger tin.
